newsitem.title: GERMANY: Strauss-Kahn confident France to meet EMU target.
newsitem.headline: Strauss-Kahn confident France to meet EMU target.

text.p: France will make great strides this year to reduce its deficit and qualify for Europe's planned single currency, French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said in an interview with the weekly Die Zeit.

Strass-Kahn said in a text of the interview made available ahead of publication on Thursday, that France's budget deficit could be lower than the Maastricht target of three percent of GDP this year, and that Portugal, Italy and Spain would likely be in the first wave of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
Strauss-Kahn said the new Socialist government in Paris would do everything it could to meet the Maastricht targets, but that it had inherited a bloated budget deficit.
"You can be certain that the budget for 1998 will be drafted with a deficit of three percent," he said.

He also added weight to the belief that a broad economic and monetary union was likely, a view that has led financial markets to speculate that the euro would be weaker than the mark at its start in 1999.

This has contributed to a pounding of Europe's anchor currency on financial markets, where the dollar hit fresh 71-month highs on Wednesday and was hovering just below 1.83 marks in late morning trade.

Strauss-Kahn said he hoped many European countries would qualify to join the first wave of monetary union when the European Union decides early next year who makes the grade, based on economic performance in 1997.

"The Benelux countries will certainly be there," he said. "Portugal, Spain and Italy as well, I think. I am convinced that the euro can become a truly European currency and not just a Franco-German currency. That would be far too narrow," he said.
Strauss-Kahn also came out in support of launching the euro on schedule and alleged that those who called for a delay of monetary union were really working towards derailing the project altogether.
"We can introduce the euro on schedule and therefore we should do it," he said.

"Whoever considers the euro to be a bad thing shouldn't talk of delay but should put his cards on the table. I, on the other hand, think the euro is a good thing and therefore want to launch it at the agreed time."
Strauss-Kahn added that he did not believe a delay of monetary union was legally possible.

Echoing arguments often used by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his finance minister Theo Waigel, Strauss-Kahn warned that a delay of monetary union could lead to turbulence on financial markets and hit European competitiveness.
"Europe needs the euro. Otherwise we cannot match the monetary power of the U.S.," he said.
Commenting on the current weakness of the mark, Strauss-Kahn rejected the assumption that the euro would be a weaker currency.
"All indications are that the euro will be a stable currency," he said. "France has had a hard currency for 15 years and Germany too, of course. Why should this change?" he asked.

He also rejected speculation that France's insistence on more coordination of European economic policies and a focus on jobs meant that Paris wanted to curb the independence of the future European central bank.

"But still I don't know how the European central bank will function if it exists in a vacuum and no political partner to consult," he said. "In every country with an independent central bank there is also a government that defines economic policies."
